seo.title: E-E-A-T for AI Search: Build Trust That Gets Cited
seo.meta_description: E-E-A-T for AI search: what experience, expertise, authoritativeness and trust mean, why Google says trust matters most, and practical steps for your site.

h1: E-E-A-T for AI Search: How to Show the Trust AI Systems Look For
answer: E-E-A-T for AI search means showing experience, expertise, authoritativeness and trustworthiness in ways both people and AI systems can see. Google says trust is the most important part. In practice that means named authors with real credentials, first-hand experience, accurate and sourced claims, transparent business details and a reputation corroborated by other sites.
key_takeaways: E-E-A-T stands for experience, expertise, authoritativeness and trust.
Google says trust is the most important of the four.
AI answers built on search inherit these quality signals.
Show who wrote content and why they are qualified.
Back claims with sources and first-hand evidence.

sections.heading: What E-E-A-T means
sections.body_html:
E-E-A-T is a framework Google uses to describe what makes content helpful and reliable. Google's guidance says its systems identify a mix of factors that indicate experience, expertise, authoritativeness and trustworthiness, and that of these, trust is most important. The others contribute to trust, but content does not have to show all of them; some content is helpful because of first-hand experience, other content because of formal expertise.

  • Experience: first-hand involvement with the topic.
  • Expertise: knowledge or skill in the subject.
  • Authoritativeness: being a recognized source on the topic.
  • Trust: being accurate, honest, safe and reliable.

sections.heading: Why it matters for AI answers
sections.body_html: Google's AI Overviews and AI Mode are built on Google's search systems, and Google says the best practices for SEO remain relevant to them. Other assistants also prefer reliable sources when they can. When an AI has to choose which passage to repeat, a page from an identifiable, qualified source with accurate, sourced claims is a safer choice than an anonymous page with unsupported claims.

sections.heading: Show experience
sections.body_html: First-hand experience is the easiest signal to add and the hardest for competitors to copy. Include what you actually did: the steps you took, what happened, what you learned, photos of real work, screenshots of real results shared with permission. A guide written by someone who has done the work reads differently from one assembled from other articles, and it contains details no one else has.

sections.heading: Show expertise
sections.body_html: Name the author of every substantial page and link to an author page that explains their background, credentials and experience. For topics that affect health, finances or safety, have qualified professionals write or review content and show the reviewer's name and the review date. Expertise should be visible, not just claimed in an About page.

sections.heading: Build authority
sections.body_html: Authority comes largely from outside your site: mentions in respected publications, citations by other experts, reviews, awards and memberships. Focus on a clear topic area so your reputation builds in one place, publish consistently on it, and earn coverage through original data and expert commentary. Authority accumulates slowly; consistency matters more than bursts.

sections.heading: Earn trust above all
sections.body_html:
• Accuracy: check facts, cite sources, update or remove outdated claims.
  • Transparency: clear business name, address, contact details and ownership.
  • Honesty: say who your advice is not for and disclose relationships or sponsorships.
  • Security: HTTPS, clear privacy policy, safe forms.
  • Customer trust: genuine reviews and a visible way to get support.

sections.heading: Who, how and why
sections.body_html: Google's helpful content guidance encourages asking who created the content, how it was created and why. For content made with automation or AI assistance, Google suggests being clear about how it was produced where readers would reasonably expect it. The underlying test is whether the content exists primarily to help people rather than to attract search visits.

sections.heading: Structured data and consistency
sections.body_html: Organization structured data with your logo and official profiles, and Article structured data with author information, help machines connect your content to your brand and authors. Keep author names, titles and company details consistent across your site, social profiles and publications so AI systems can link them reliably.

sections.heading: A quick E-E-A-T audit
sections.body_html:
1. Does every key page show who wrote or reviewed it?
  2. Do author pages explain relevant experience and credentials?
  3. Are claims supported by sources or first-hand evidence?
  4. Is it easy to find who runs the business and how to contact them?
  5. Are pages updated when facts change?
  6. Do independent sites mention and recommend you?

sections.heading: What E-E-A-T is not
sections.body_html: E-E-A-T is not a single score or a checklist that guarantees rankings. Adding an author bio to a weak page will not make it helpful. It is a description of qualities that good content tends to have, so the most reliable way to improve it is to make content that genuinely is experienced, expert, authoritative and trustworthy.

sections.heading: An example of adding E-E-A-T to a page
sections.body_html: Take a generic page titled "Tips for choosing a contractor". To improve it, the business adds the author's name and role with a link to their profile, replaces general tips with lessons from jobs the team has completed, includes photos of real work, cites the state licensing board for how to check a license, adds a clear date and a note on when it was last reviewed, and links to the company's contact and licensing details. Nothing in the topic changed, but the page now shows who stands behind it and why they are worth listening to.

sections.heading: E-E-A-T for small businesses
sections.body_html: Small businesses often worry they cannot compete on authority with large brands. They can compete on experience and trust: local knowledge, real customer stories, owners who answer questions personally, and transparent pricing. These are signals large publishers often lack, and they are exactly what makes content useful for local and specialist questions.

faqs.a: Experience, expertise, authoritativeness and trustworthiness. Google uses the framework to describe qualities of helpful, reliable content, and says trust is the most important.
Google describes E-E-A-T as qualities its systems look for through a mix of factors, not a single score. Improving the underlying qualities is what helps.

faqs.q: Does E-E-A-T matter for AI Overviews?
faqs.a: Google says SEO best practices remain relevant to AI features, and its systems aim to prioritize helpful, reliable content, so trust signals matter there too.

faqs.q: How do I show experience on a page?
faqs.a: Describe what you actually did, include real examples, photos or results shared with permission, and share details only someone with first-hand involvement would know.

faqs.q: Do author bios help with AI search?
faqs.a: Named authors with relevant credentials make expertise visible and help connect content to real people, which supports trust. A bio cannot fix weak content, though.

faqs.q: Which topics need the most E-E-A-T?
faqs.a: Topics that can affect health, finances, safety or major decisions need the strongest evidence of expertise and trust.

faqs.q: Can AI-assisted content have good E-E-A-T?
faqs.a: Yes, if it is accurate, reviewed by people with real expertise, adds first-hand insight and exists to help readers rather than to manipulate rankings.
